## Research overview

### Bacterial synthesis of metal nanoparticles

Environmental bacteria — *Acinetobacter* species in particular — can be induced to
reduce metal salts into nanoparticles of controlled size and shape. My doctoral and
subsequent work established the conditions under which this happens, identified
lignin peroxidase and a purified protein fraction as agents of the reduction, and
characterised the silver, gold and selenium particles that result. The appeal is
that the synthesis runs in water, at room temperature, without the reducing agents
that conventional routes depend on.

### What the particles are good for

Biogenic nanoparticles turn out to be active where conventional antimicrobials are
struggling. We have shown silver nanoparticles disrupting *Acinetobacter* biofilms,
acting in synergy with existing antibiotics against nosocomial strains, working
against *Candida albicans*, and — with phytogenic silver and gold particles —
against *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. Selenium nanoparticles from *Acinetobacter*
sp. SW30 proved cytotoxic to breast cancer cells.

### Cleaning up: dyes, microplastics and waste as a resource

Textile dye in water is both a pollutant and a convenient test substrate. Recent
work uses banana and carrot peel waste as a biosorbent for procion magenta and
black azabache dyes, and gold nanocatalysts to decolorise dye effluent. A current
review thread asks whether nano-adsorbents can be made to capture microplastics.

### Science education

A parallel strand, with colleagues at SIES, looks at how teachers actually learn —
the effect of online professional courses on teaching practice, experiential
learning that blends MOOCs with project work and internships, and how public
understanding of food-contact materials shifts with education.
